Visualise 3D shapes, bond angles and electron density; predict properties.
Collect many readings at precise intervals (fast or long experiments), reduce human reading errors, and allow real-time graphs.

front: Shape of a calibration curve of absorbance vs concentration?
back: Straight line through the origin at low concentrations (Beer–Lambert law); may curve at high concentration.
Process raw data with formulas (means, uncertainties), plot graphs, add trendlines and compute gradients/intercepts and R².
Retrieve secondary data (e.g. enthalpies, Ka values, spectra) to compare with or extend experimental results; cite the source.

front: Why use computer simulations in chemistry?
back: Explore systems that are dangerous, expensive, too fast/slow or sub-microscopic (e.g. kinetics, gas behaviour, equilibrium) and test models.

front: Why use a temperature probe in calorimetry?
back: Records temperature continuously so the cooling curve can be extrapolated to find the true maximum ΔT.

front: Using a conductivity probe in a titration?
back: Conductivity changes as ions are replaced (e.g. H⁺ by Na⁺); the end point is at the minimum/change in gradient — useful for coloured solutions.

front: Using a pH probe with a data logger in a titration?
back: Plots the full pH curve, giving the equivalence point and pKa (half-equivalence) without an indicator.

front: Using a pressure sensor in rate experiments?
back: In a sealed flask, pressure rise is proportional to gas produced, so the rate can be followed with time.

front: How are spectral databases used to identify a compound?
back: Compare the measured IR/MS/¹H NMR spectrum with reference spectra of known compounds for a match.
They simplify reality (e.g. ball-and-stick shows no electron clouds; space-filling hides bond angles); predictions must be tested experimentally.

front: What should you check when adding a spreadsheet trendline?
back: Correct model (linear vs curve), whether forcing through origin is justified, R² value, and outliers; include uncertainty (error) bars.

front: Choosing a data logger sampling rate?
back: High enough to capture rapid changes (fast reactions), low enough not to produce excessive data for slow processes.

front: Does a data logger make data more accurate?
back: Not automatically — it is only as accurate as the calibrated sensor; it improves precision of timing and reduces reading errors.

front: What can computer modelling show that VSEPR cannot?
back: Electron density/electrostatic potential maps showing polarity, and calculated bond lengths and energies.
